To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

a lineup may be used as an instrument to screen for consumers with high valuations for the ticket, and that the monopolist may charge a price that is above the consumer surplus of the consumers who buy tickets.

a lineup is a screening device for the monopolist, and that a lineup is more likely to be used by the monopolist if the monopolist's cost of serving a consumer increases with the number of other customers served.

a lineup is used by a monopolist as a screening mechanism when a consumer's willingness to pay depends negatively on the number of consumers who line up before her, and that a lineup is also used as a mechanism for price discrimination in the case of a capacity constraint.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the following question: What are the conditions under which an individual's willingness to pay depends upon the willingness to pay of others?
the following questions: (1) When is the use of lineups optimal for a firm that is a monopolist or a price taker?
the question of how the market for tickets can be made to work efficiently.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
, for a monopolist, a lineup is not a good screening mechanism.
the monopolist will never use a lineup as screening mechanism if there is no capacity constraint.

, in a market with excess demand, a seller can use a lineup as an instrument to extract more revenue by screening consumers, and that the seller will do so if the consumer's cost of lining up is negatively related to her value of attending the event.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the monopolist's optimal policy is to use a lineup when the cost of lining up is high, and to charge a high price and a capacity constraint when the cost of queuing is low.

the monopolist's optimal lineup is a function of the consumer's cost of lining up, the consumer's cost for waiting in the lineup, and the consumer's valuation of the good, all of which depend on the consumer's characteristic.
the monopolist's pricing and capacity decisions are affected not only by the characteristics of the marginal attendee, but also by the characteristics of other attendees.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the monopolist can use the lineup to screen consumers for their willingness to pay.
the existence of a lineup is not a reliable signal of excess demand.
the presence of a queue can affect the pricing strategy of an event organizer.
